data.text:
USS Pennsylvania and battleship of Colorado class followed by three cruisers move in line into Lingayen Gulf preceding the landing on Luzon. Philippines, January 1945.

In January 1945, U.S. forces launched the invasion of Luzon, the largest and most strategically important island in the Philippines. To pave the way, powerful naval task forces entered Lingayen Gulf under heavy Japanese resistance.

USS Pennsylvania (BB-38), a veteran battleship of Pearl Harbor, led the way alongside ships of the Colorado-class and several cruisers. Their mission was to bombard Japanese coastal defences, clear mines, and provide covering fire for the landing forces. The approach was hazardous—Japanese aircraft, including kamikazes, repeatedly attacked the fleet, inflicting serious damage on several ships.

Despite these dangers, the naval bombardment was highly effective. It neutralized many Japanese strongpoints and allowed General MacArthur’s forces to land on 9 January 1945 with overwhelming strength. The operation marked a decisive step in the liberation of the Philippines, cutting Japan off from vital resources in Southeast Asia and bringing Allied forces closer to the Japanese homeland.
